- Since `Rust 2018`edition, you need to declare`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`per module. Before you would write`#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions;`.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.
- `assert_ne`is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does- *not*show a diff.
- Under Windows, the terminal state is modified to properly handle VT100 escape sequences, which may break display for certain use cases.
- The minimum supported rust version (MSRV) is 1.35.0

`no_std` support

For `no_std` support, disable the `std` feature and enable the `alloc` feature:

```
# Cargo.toml
 = { = "...",  = false,  = ["alloc"] }
```

# Pretty Assertions

When writing tests in Rust, you'll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` *a lot*.

If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`, but you have to spot, the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward, like here:

Wouldn't that task be *much* easier with a colorful diff?

Yep — and you only need **one line of code** to make it happen:

```
 extern crate pretty_assertions;
```
```
// 1. add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
// 2. insert this line at the top of your crate root or integration test
 extern crate pretty_assertions;
```
## Tip

Specify it as [ [dev-dependencies]](http://doc.crates.io/specifying-dependencies.html#development-dependencies)
and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
This way the compile time of

`cargo build` won't be affected!In your crate root, also add `#[cfg(test)]` to the crate import, like this:

```
 // <-- not needed in examples + integration tests
extern crate pretty_assertions;
```
## Note

- Each example and integration test also needs `#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions`, if you want colorful diffs there.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.
- `assert_ne`is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does- *not*show a diff.

and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
This way the compile time of

`cargo build` won't be affected!In your crate root, also add `#[cfg(test)]` to the crate import, like this:

```
 // <-- not needed in examples + integration tests
extern crate pretty_assertions;
```
## Note

- Each example and integration test also needs `#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions`, if you want colorful diffs there.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.
- `assert_ne`is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does- *not*show a diff.

# pretty_assertions 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty_assertions/0.1.0

# Pretty Assertions

When writing tests in Rust, you'll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` *a lot*.

If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`, but you have to spot, the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward, like here:

Wouldn't that task be *much* easier with a colorful diff?

Yes it would. And you only need **one line of code** to make it happen —
seriously:

```
// add the following line to the top of your crate root to
// overwrite `assert_eq!` with a colorful drop-in replacement
 extern crate pretty_assertions;
```
Ok, and don't forget to add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
Does that count as a line of code?.. ;-)

## Note

- `pretty_assertions`is an ultra-thin wrapper around the- `difference`- `assert_eq!`macro with just about 22 lines of code.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.

## Example

This is the Rust code behind the screenshots above.

```
// uncomment the next line to make the assertions colorful:
//#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions;
```

# pretty_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pretty_assertions

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#pretty-assertions)Pretty Assertions

When writing tests in Rust, you’ll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` *a lot*.

If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`.
But you have to spot the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward,
like here:

Wouldn’t that task be *much* easier with a colorful diff?

Yep — and you only need **one line of code** to make it happen:

`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`## Show the example behind the screenshots above.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// 1. add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
// 2. insert this line at the top of each module, as needed
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Foo {
    lorem: &'static str,
    ipsum: u32,
    dolor: Result<String, String>,
}
let x = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello World!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey".to_string())});
let y = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello Wrold!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey ho!".to_string())});
assert_eq!(x, y);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#tip)Tip

Specify it as [ [dev-dependencies]](http://doc.crates.io/specifying-dependencies.html#development-dependencies)
and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
This way the compile time of

`cargo build` won’t be affected!Also add `#[cfg(test)]` to your `use` statements, like this:

```
#[cfg(test)]
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

- Since `Rust 2018`edition, you need to declare`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`per module. Before you would write`#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions;`.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.
- `assert_ne`is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does- *not*show a diff.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Features provided by the crate are:

- `std`: Use the Rust standard library. Enabled by default. Exactly one of- `std`and- `alloc`is required.
- `alloc`: Use the- `alloc`crate. Exactly one of- `std`and- `alloc`is required.
- `unstable`: opt-in to unstable features that may not follow Semantic Versioning. The implementation behind this feature is subject to change without warning between patch versions.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq.html)- eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_matches.html)- matches
- Asserts that a value matches a pattern.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_ne.html)- ne
- Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_str_eq.html)- str_ - eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using `PartialEq`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Comparison](https://docs.rs/struct.Comparison.html)
- A comparison of two values.
- [StrComparison](https://docs.rs/struct.StrComparison.html)
- A comparison of two strings.

# pretty_assertions 1.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty_assertions/latest/source/README.md

```
[![Latest version](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/pretty-assertions.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/pretty-assertions)
[![docs.rs](https://img.shields.io/docsrs/pretty_assertions)](https://docs.rs/pretty_assertions)
[![Downloads of latest version](https://img.shields.io/crates/dv/pretty-assertions.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/pretty-assertions)
[![All downloads](https://img.shields.io/crates/d/pretty-assertions.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/pretty-assertions)
Overwrite `assert_eq!` with a drop-in replacement, adding a colorful diff.
When writing tests in Rust, you'll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` _a lot_.
If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`.
But you have to spot the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward,
like here:
![standard assertion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rust-pretty-assertions/rust-pretty-assertions/2d2357ff56d22c51a86b2f1cfe6efcee9f5a8081/examples/standard_assertion.png)
Wouldn't that task be _much_ easier with a colorful diff?
![pretty assertion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rust-pretty-assertions/rust-pretty-assertions/2d2357ff56d22c51a86b2f1cfe6efcee9f5a8081/examples/pretty_assertion.png)
Yep — and you only need **one line of code** to make it happen:
```rust,ignore
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
```
```rust,ignore
// 1. add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
// 2. insert this line at the top of each module, as needed
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
fn main() {
}
```
The exact output of assertions is **not guaranteed** to be consistent over time, and may change between minor versions.
The output of this crate is designed to be read by a human. It is not suitable for exact comparison, for example in snapshot testing.
This crate adheres to semantic versioning for publically exported crate items, **except** the `private` module, which may change between any version.
Specify it as [`[dev-dependencies]`](http://doc.crates.io/specifying-dependencies.html#development-dependencies)
and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
This way the compile time of `cargo build` won't be affected!
Also add `#[cfg(test)]` to your `use` statements, like this:
```rust,ignore
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
```
- ----
For `no_std` support, disable the `std` feature and enable the `alloc` feature:
```toml
pretty_assertions = { version= "...", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```

# criterion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/criterion/^0.3.5/

## Expand description

A statistics-driven micro-benchmarking library written in Rust.

This crate is a microbenchmarking library which aims to provide strong statistical confidence in detecting and estimating the size of performance improvements and regressions, while also being easy to use.

See
[the user guide](https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/index.html)
for examples as well as details on the measurement and analysis process,
and the output.

- Collects detailed statistics, providing strong confidence that changes to performance are real, not measurement noise.
- Produces detailed charts, providing thorough understanding of your code’s performance behavior.

This module defines a trait that can be used to plug in different Futures executors into Criterion.rs’ async benchmarking support.

This module defines a set of traits that can be used to plug different measurements (eg.
Unix’s Processor Time, CPU or GPU performance counters, etc.) into Criterion.rs. It also
includes the [WallTime](https://docs.rs/struct.WallTime.html) struct which defines the default wall-clock time
measurement.

This module provides an extension trait which allows in-process profilers
to be hooked into the `--profile-time` argument at compile-time. Users of
out-of-process profilers such as perf don’t need to do anything special.

Macro used to define a function group for the benchmark harness; see the
`criterion_main!` macro for more details.

Structure used to group together a set of related benchmarks, along with custom configuration settings for groups of benchmarks. All benchmarks performed using a benchmark group will be grouped together in the final report.

Simple structure representing an ID for a benchmark. The ID must be unique within a benchmark group.

This enum allows the user to control how Criterion.rs chooses the iteration count when sampling. The default is Auto, which will choose a method automatically based on the iteration time during the warm-up phase.

Enum representing different ways of measuring the throughput of benchmarked code. If the throughput setting is configured for a benchmark then the estimated throughput will be reported as well as the time per iteration.

# quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/^1.0.3/

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/macro.quickcheck.html)
- A macro for writing quickcheck tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)
- `Gen`represents a PRNG.
- [NoShrink](https://docs.rs/struct.NoShrink.html)
- Wrapper for disabling shrinking for an Arbitrary
- [Quick](https://docs.rs/struct.QuickCheck.html)- Check
- The main `QuickCheck`type for setting configuration and running`QuickCheck`.
- [Test](https://docs.rs/struct.TestResult.html)- Result
- Describes the status of a single instance of a test.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- `Arbitrary`describes types whose values can be randomly generated and shrunk.
- [Testable](https://docs.rs/trait.Testable.html)
- `Testable`describes types (e.g., a function) whose values can be tested.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with zero elements.
- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/fn.quickcheck.html)
- Convenience function for running `QuickCheck`.
- [single_](https://docs.rs/fn.single_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with a single element.

# yansi 1.0.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/yansi/1.0.1

## Usage

In your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
In your source code:

```
use Paint;
println!;
```
[See the rustdocs](https://docs.rs/yansi) for complete usage details.

## Features

Why *y*et another *ANSI* terminal coloring library? Here are some reasons:

- This library makes simple things *simple*:`use``Paint`
- Zero dependencies by default. It really is simple.
- Zero allocations except as needed by opt-in [wrapping](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/#wrapping).
- [Automatic Windows support](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/#windows)for the vast majority (95%+) of Windows users.
- [Featureful](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/#crate-features), no-- `no_std`- `alloc`, support with- `default-features = false`.
- `Style`constructors are- `const`
- *Any*type implementing a formatting trait can be styled, not just strings.
- Styling can be [enabled](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/fn.enable.html)and[disabled](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/fn.disable.html)globally and[dynamically](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/fn.whenever.html), on the fly.
- A `Style`can be predicated on arbitrary[conditions](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/#per-style).
- Formatting specifiers like `{:x}`and`{:08b}`are supported and preserved!
- [Built-in (optional) conditions](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions)for- [TTY detection](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-1)and- [common environment variables](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-2).
- Arbitrary items can be *masked*
- Styling can *wrap*
- Styling can *linger*
- Experimental support for [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/yansi/1.0.0/yansi/hyperlink/index.html)is included.
- The name `yansi`is pretty cool 😎.

## License

`yansi` is licensed under either of the following, at your option:

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT License ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

# is_terminal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/is-terminal/^0.4.11/

## Expand description

is-terminal is a simple utility that answers one question:

Is this a terminal?

A “terminal”, also known as a “tty”, is an I/O device which may be interactive and may support color and other special features. This crate doesn’t provide any of those features; it just answers this one question.

On Unix-family platforms, this is effectively the same as the [ isatty](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/isatty.3.html)
function for testing whether a given stream is a terminal, though it
accepts high-level stream types instead of raw file descriptors.

On Windows, it uses a variety of techniques to determine whether the given stream is a terminal.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use is_terminal::IsTerminal;
if std::io::stdout().is_terminal() {
    println!("stdout is a terminal")
}
```
## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [IsTerminal](https://docs.rs/trait.IsTerminal.html)
- Extension trait to check whether something is a terminal.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_terminal.html)- terminal
- Returns `true`if`this`is a terminal.

---

# yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/yansi/1.0.1/target-redirect/yansi/

## Expand description

A dead simple ANSI terminal color painting library.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Why *y*et another *ANSI* terminal coloring library? Here are some reasons:

- This library makes simple things *simple*:`use``Paint`
- Zero dependencies by default. It really is simple.
- Zero allocations except as needed by opt-in [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping).
- [Automatic Windows support](https://docs.rs#windows)for the vast majority (95%+) of Windows users.
- [Featureful](https://docs.rs#crate-features), no-- `no_std`- `alloc`, support with- `default-features = false`.
- `Style`constructors are- `const`
- *Any*type implementing a formatting trait can be styled, not just strings.
- Styling can be [enabled](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html)and[disabled](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)globally and[dynamically](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html), on the fly.
- A `Style`can be predicated on arbitrary[conditions](https://docs.rs#per-style).
- Formatting specifiers like `{:x}`and`{:08b}`are supported and preserved!
- [Built-in (optional) conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions)for- [TTY detection](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-1)and- [common environment variables](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-2).
- Arbitrary items can be *masked*
- Styling can *wrap*
- Styling can *linger*
- Experimental support for [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)is included.
- The name `yansi`is pretty cool 😎.

All that said, `yansi` borrows API ideas from older libraries as well as
implementation details from [ ansi_term](https://crates.io/crates/ansi_term).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The [ Paint](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html) trait is implemented for every type. Import it and call
chainable builder methods:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
    "Ready".bold(),
    "Set".yellow().italic(),
    "STOP".white().on_red().bright().underline().bold());
```
`>` Testing,
**Ready**,
* Set*,

__!__

use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*};
// `const` constructors allow static `Style`s for easy reuse
static ALERT: Style = White.bright().underline().italic().on_red();
println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
    "Ready".bold(),

[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-styling)Conditional Styling

[§](https://docs.rs#globally)Globally

Styling is enabled by default but can be enabled and disabled globally via
[ enable()](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html) and

[. When styling is disabled, no ANSI escape codes are emitted, and](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)

`disable()`[values are omitted entirely.](https://docs.rs#masking)

*masked*Global styling can also be dynamically enabled and disabled using
[ whenever()](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html) with an arbitrary

[: a function that returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html)

`Condition``true` or `false`. This condition is evaluated each time a [item is displayed. The associated styling is enabled, and mask values emitted, exactly when and only when the condition returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``true`.[§](https://docs.rs#per-style)Per-`Style`

A specific `Style` can itself be conditionally applied by using
[ .whenever()](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.whenever):

```
use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*, Condition};
static WARNING: Style = Black.bold().on_yellow().whenever(Condition::STDERR_IS_TTY);
eprintln!("{}", "Bees can sting!".paint(WARNING));
```
With the above, if `stderr` is a TTY, then:
`>` **Bees can sting!**

If it is not a TTY, styling is not emitted:
`>` Bees can sting!

See [ Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html) for a list of built-in conditions which require enabling
crate features.

[§](https://docs.rs#quirks)Quirks

As a convenience, `yansi` implements several “quirks”, applicable via
[ Quirk](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html) and the respective methods, that modify if and how styling is
presented to the terminal. These quirks do not correspond to any ANSI
styling sequences.

[§](https://docs.rs#masking)Masking

Items can be arbitrarily *masked* with the [ mask()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#tymethod.mask) builder
method. Masked values are not emitted when styling is disabled, globally or
for a given style. This allows selective output based on whether styling is
enabled.

One use for this feature is to print certain characters only when styling is enabled. For instance, you might wish to emit the 🎨 emoji when coloring is enabled but not otherwise. This can be accomplished by masking the emoji:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("I like colors!{}", " 🎨".mask());
```
When styling is enabled, this prints: `>` I like colors! 🎨

With styling disabled, this prints: `>` I like colors!

[§](https://docs.rs#wrapping)Wrapping

**Note:** *Either the  std or alloc feature is required for wrapping.
std is enabled by default. See *

[crate features](https://docs.rs#crate-features).

Styling can *wrap* via [ Quirk::Wrap](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Wrap) or the equivalent

[constructor. A wrapping style modifies any styling resets emitted by the internal value so that they correspond to the wrapping style. In other words, the “reset” style of the wrapped item is modified to be the style being](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.wrap)

`wrap()``.wrap()`d.Wrapping is useful in situations where opaque and arbitrary values must be styled consistently irrespective of any existing styling. For example, a generic logger might want to style messages based on log levels consistently, even when those messages may already include styling. Wrapping exists to enable such consistent styling:

```
use yansi::Paint;
// Imagine that `inner` is opaque and we don't know it's styling.
let inner = format!("{} and {}", "Stop".red(), "Go".green());
// We can use `wrap` to ensure anything in `inner` not styled is blue.
println!("Hey! {}", inner.blue().wrap());
```
Thanks to wrapping, this prints:
`>` Hey!
Stop and
Go

Without wrapping, the reset after `"Stop".red()` would not be overwritten:
`>` Hey! Stop and Go

Wrapping incurs a performance cost due to an extra allocation and replacement if the wrapped item has styling applied to it. Otherwise, it does not allocate nor incur a meaningful performance cost.

[§](https://docs.rs#lingering)Lingering

Styling can *linger* beyond a single value via [ Quirk::Linger](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Linger) or the
equivalent

[constructor. A lingering style does not reset itself after being applied. In other words, the style lingers on beyond the value it’s applied to, until something else resets the respective styling.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.linger)

`linger()`The complement to lingering is force resetting via [ Quirk::Resetting](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Resetting) or
the equivalent

[constructor. Force resetting, as the name implies, forces a reset suffix to be emitted after the value, irrespective of any lingering applied. It can be used as a way to finalize a lingering style.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.resetting)

`resetting()`Lingering itself is useful in situations where a given style is to be
repeated across multiple values, or when style is intended to persist even
across values that are not styled with `yansi`. It also allows avoiding
unnecessarily repeated ANSI code sequences. The examples below illustrate
some scenarios in which lingering is useful:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic().linger(),
    "you".on_yellow(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "today".blue());
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are things with you__
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "you".on_yellow().linger(),
    "today".blue()); // doesn't linger; styling is reset
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are__
things with
you
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("{} B {} {} {} F",
    "A".red().linger(),
    "C".underline().linger(),
    "D", // doesn't linger, but no styling applied, thus no reset
    "E".resetting());  // explicitly reset
```
`>`  A B __C D E__  F

[§](https://docs.rs#brightening)Brightening

Most pimrary colors are available in regular and *bright* variants, e.g.,
[ Color::Red](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.Red) and

[. The](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.BrightRed)

`Color::BrightRed`[and](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Bright)

`Quirk::Bright`[quirks, typically applied via](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.OnBright)

`Quirk::OnBright`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.bright)

`.bright()`[, provide an alternative, convenient mechanism to select the bright variant of the selected foreground or background color, respectively. The quirk provides no additional colors and is equivalent to selecting the bright variants directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.on_bright)

`.on_bright()````
use yansi::Paint;
// These are all equivalent.
print!("{}", "Regular".red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright_red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright().red());
print!("{}", "Bright".red().bright());
// The `bright` quirk lets use choose the bright variants of _any_ color,
// even when the color or style is unknown at the call site.
print!("{}", "Normal".paint(STYLE));
print!("{}", "Bright".paint(STYLE).bright());
```
`>` Regular
Bright
Bright
Bright
**Normal**
**Bright**

The `bright()` quirk can be applied before or after a color is selected
while having the same effect.

[§](https://docs.rs#windows)Windows

Styling is supported and enabled automatically on Windows beginning with
the Windows 10 Anniversary Update, or about [96% of all Windows machines
worldwide](https://gs.statcounter.com/os-version-market-share/windows/desktop/worldwide),
and likely closer to 100% of developer machines (e.g., 99% of visitors to
[rocket.rs](https://rocket.rs) on Windows are on Windows 10+).

Yansi enables styling support on Windows by querying the Windows API on the first attempt to color. If support is available, it is enabled. If support is not available, styling is disabled and no styling sequences are emitted.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

| Feature | Default? | Also Enables | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std` | Y | `alloc` | Use `std`library. |
| `alloc` | Y | Use `alloc`. Enables[wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping). | |
| `detect-tty` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `detect-env` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `hyperlink` | N | `std` | Enables [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)support. |

With `default-features = false`, this crate is `#[no_std]`.

Without any features enabled, all functionality except [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping) is
available. To recover wrapping *with* `#[no_std]`, set `default-features = false` and enable the `alloc` feature, which requires `alloc` support.

}## Expand description

A trait to apply styling to any value. Implemented for all types.

Because this trait is implemented for all types, you can use its methods on
any type. With the exception of one constructor method, [ Paint::new()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.new),
all methods are called with method syntax:

```
use yansi::Paint;
"hello".green(); // calls `Paint::<&'static str>::green()`.
"hello".strike(); // calls `Paint::<&'static str>::strike()`.
1.on_red(); // calls `Paint::<i32>::red()`.
1.blink(); // calls `Paint::<i32>::blink()`.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#chaining)Chaining

All methods return a [ Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html) whose methods are exactly those of

`Paint`.
This means you can chain `Paint` method calls:```
use yansi::Paint;
"hello".green().strike(); // calls `Paint::green()` then `Painted::strike()`.
1.on_red().blink(); // calls `Paint::red()` + `Painted::blink()`.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#borrow-vs-owned-receiver)Borrow vs. Owned Receiver

The returned [ Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html) type contains a borrow to the receiver:

```
use yansi::{Paint, Painted};
let v: Painted<&i32> = 1.red();
```
This is nearly always what you want. In the exceedingly rare case that you
*do* want `Painted` to own its value, use [ Paint::new()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.new) or the equivalent

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.new)

`Painted::new()````
use yansi::{Paint, Painted};
let v: Painted<i32> = Paint::new(1);
let v: Painted<i32> = Painted::new(1);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#further-details)Further Details

See the [crate level docs](https://docs.rs/index.html#usage) for more details and examples.

# enable in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/^1.0.1/fn.enable.html

`pub fn enable()`## Expand description

Unconditionally enables styling globally.

By default, styling is enabled based on [ Condition::DEFAULT](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#associatedconstant.DEFAULT), which checks
for operating system support.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yansi::Paint;
// With styling disabled, ANSI color codes are _not_ emitted.
yansi::disable();
assert_eq!("go".green().to_string(), "go".to_string());
// Reenabling causes color code to be emitted.
yansi::enable();
assert_ne!("go".green().to_string(), "go".to_string());
```

---

# disable in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/^1.0.1/fn.disable.html

`pub fn disable()`## Expand description

Unconditionally disables styling globally.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yansi::Paint;
// With styling enabled, ANSI color codes are emitted, thus `ne`.
assert_ne!("go".green().to_string(), "go".to_string());
// With styling disabled, ANSI color codes are _not_ emitted.
yansi::disable();
assert_eq!("go".green().to_string(), "go".to_string());
```

# whenever in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/^1.0.1/fn.whenever.html

`pub fn whenever(condition: `[Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html))## Expand description

Dynamically enables and disables styling globally based on `condition`.

`condition` is expected to be fast: it is checked dynamically, each time a
[ Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html) value is displayed.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yansi::Condition;
yansi::whenever(Condition::STDOUT_IS_TTY);
// On each styling, check if we have TTYs.
yansi::whenever(Condition::STDOUTERR_ARE_TTY_LIVE);
// Check `NO_COLOR`, `CLICOLOR`, and if we have TTYs.
const HAVE_COLOR: Condition = Condition(|| {
    std::env::var_os("NO_COLOR").is_none()
        && (Condition::CLICOLOR_LIVE)()
        && Condition::stdouterr_are_tty_live()
});
// This will call `HAVE_COLOR` every time styling is needed. In this
// example, this means that env vars will be checked on each styling.
yansi::whenever(HAVE_COLOR);
// This instead caches the value (checking `env()` exactly once, now).
yansi::whenever(Condition::cached((HAVE_COLOR)()));
// Is identical to this:
match (HAVE_COLOR)() {
    true => yansi::enable(),
    false => yansi::disable(),
}
```

# Condition in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/^1.0.1/struct.Condition.html

## Expand description

A function that decides whether styling should be applied.

A styling `Condition` can be specified globally via
[ yansi::whenever()](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html) or locally to a specific style via
the

[builder method. Any time a](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.whenever)

`whenever()`[value is formatted, both the local and global conditions are checked, and only when both evaluate to](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``true` is styling
actually applied.A `Condition` is nothing more than a function that returns a `bool`. The
function is called each and every time a `Painted` is formatted, and so it
is expected to be fast. All of the built-in conditions (except for their
“live” variants) cache their first evaluation as a result: the
[ Condition::cached()](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#method.cached) constructor can do the same for your conditions.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-conditions)Built-In Conditions

`yansi` comes with built-in conditions for common scenarios that can be
enabled via crate features:

| feature(s) | condition | implication |
|---|---|---|
| `detect-tty` | [TTY Detectors](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-1) | `std`,`is-terminal` |
| `detect-env` | [Environment Variable Checkers](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-2) | `std` |
| [ `detect-tty`,`detect-env`] | All Above, [Combo Detectors](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-3) | `std`,`is-terminal` |

For example, to enable the TTY detectors, enable the `detect-tty` feature:

`yansi = { version = "...", features = ["detect-tty"] }`To enable the TTY detectors, env-var checkers, and combo detectors, enable
`detect-tty` *and* `detect-env`:

`yansi = { version = "...", features = ["detect-tty", "detect-env"] }````
use yansi::Condition;
yansi::whenever(Condition::TTY_AND_COLOR);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-conditions)Custom Conditions

Custom, arbitrary conditions can be created with [ Condition::from()](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#method.from) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#method.cached)

`Condition::cached()````
use yansi::{Condition, Style, Color::*};
// Combine two conditions (`stderr` is a TTY, `CLICOLOR` is set) into one.
static STDERR_COLOR: Condition = Condition::from(||
    Condition::stderr_is_tty() && Condition::clicolor()
);
static DEBUG: Style = Yellow.bold().on_primary().invert().whenever(STDERR_COLOR);
```

A condition that evaluates to `true` if the OS supports coloring.

Uses [ Condition::os_support()](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#method.os_support). On Windows, this condition tries to
enable coloring support on the first call and caches the result for
subsequent calls. Outside of Windows, this always evaluates to

`true`.Creates a dynamically checked condition from a function `f`.

The function `f` is called anytime the condition is checked, including
every time a style with the condition is used.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yansi::Condition;
fn some_function() -> bool {
    /* checking arbitrary conditions */
    todo!()
}
// Create a custom static condition from a function.
static MY_CONDITION: Condition = Condition::from(some_function);
// Create a condition on the stack from a function.
let my_condition = Condition::from(some_function);
// Create a static condition from a closure that becomes a `fn`.
static MY_CONDITION_2: Condition = Condition::from(|| false);
// Create a condition on the stack from a closure that becomes a `fn`.
let my_condition = Condition::from(|| some_function());
```
Creates a condition that is [ ALWAYS](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#associatedconstant.ALWAYS) when

`value` is
`true` and [otherwise.](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#associatedconstant.NEVER)

`NEVER`[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use yansi::Condition;

    /* checking arbitrary conditions */

Option <Color >,

}Expand description A set of styling options.

§ Equivalence and OrderingOnly a style’s `foreground`, `background`, and set of `attributes` are
considered when testing for equivalence or producing an ordering via
`PartialEq` or `Eq`, and `PartialOrd` or `Ord`. A style’s quirks and
conditions are ignored.

The foreground color. Defaults to `None`.

use  yansi::{Style, Color};
assert_eq! (Style::new().foreground, None );
assert_eq! (Style::new().green().foreground, Some (Color::Green));The background color. Defaults to `None`.

use  yansi::{Style, Color};
assert_eq! (Style::new().background, None );
assert_eq! (Style::new().on_red().background, Some (Color::Red));The condition.

To check a style’s condition directly, use `Style::enabled()`

use  yansi::{Style, Condition};
let  style = Style::new().whenever(Condition::ALWAYS);
assert! (style.enabled());
let  style = Style::new().whenever(Condition::NEVER);
assert! (!style.enabled());Returns a new style with no foreground or background, no attributes
or quirks, and `Condition::DEFAULT`

This is the default returned by `Default::default()`

§ Exampleuse  yansi::Style;
assert_eq! (Style::new(), Style::default());Returns `true` if this style is enabled, based on
`condition`

Note:  For a style to be effected, both this method and
`yansi::is_enabled()``true`.

When there is no condition set, this method always returns `true`. When
a condition has been set, this evaluates the condition and returns the
result.

This method writes the ANSI code prefix irrespective of whether painting
is currently enabled or disabled. To write the prefix only if painting

§ Exampleuse  core::fmt;
use  yansi::Style;

    fn  fmt(& self , f: &mut  fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        self .style.fmt_prefix(f)? ;
        write! (f, "number: {}" , self .item)? ;
        self .style.fmt_suffix(f)
    }

Expand description Enum representing a terminal color.

Note:  The color examples below are purely demonstrative. The actual
color rendered depends entirely on the terminal and its configuration, the
latter of which is entirely arbitrary.

Terminal primary color #9. (foreground code `39`, background code `49`).

This is the terminal’s defined “primary” color, that is, the configured
default foreground and background colors. As such, this color as a
foreground looks “good” against the terminal’s default background color,
and this color is a “good” background color for the terminal’s default
foreground color.

A color from 0 to 255, for use in 256-color terminals.

# Quirk in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/^1.0.1/enum.Quirk.html

Enum Quirk  Copy item path  Source  ```
pub enum Quirk {
    Mask,
    Wrap,
    Linger,
    Clear,
    Resetting,
    Bright,
    OnBright,
}
```
Expand description Mask: omit when painting is disabled.

Typically applied via the `mask()`

See the crate level docs  for details.

Wrap the value: replace resets with the wrapped styling.

Typically applied via the `wrap()`

See the crate level docs  for details.

Linger: do not reset the style after it is applied.

# Attribute in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/^1.0.1/enum.Attribute.html

Enum Attribute  Copy item path  Source  ```
pub enum Attribute {
    Bold,
    Dim,
    Italic,
    Underline,
    Blink,
    RapidBlink,
    Invert,
    Conceal,
    Strike,
}
```
Expand description Enum representing text attributes, largely for text formatting.

Text attributes are typically applied to a `Style``Color``Painted``bold()``italic()`

Attributes are idempotent, so applying an attribute more than once has no
more affect than applying it once.

§ Terminal SupportWhether an applied attribute actually has an effect on how text is rendered
in a terminal depends on the terminal’s support for the attribute as well as
the terminal’s configuration. Common attributes, such as `bold`, `dim`,
`italic`, `underline`, and `strike` typically have good support and are
largely reliable. Less commonly supported attributes like `conceal` and
`invert` will usually  be supported by “modern” terminals. Rarely supported
attributes, such as  `blink` and `rapid blink`, will typically have no
effect when applied.

# is_enabled in yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/^1.0.1/fn.is_enabled.html

`pub fn is_enabled() -> `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)## Expand description

Returns `true` if styling is globally enabled and `false` otherwise.

By default, styling is enabled based on [ Condition::DEFAULT](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#associatedconstant.DEFAULT), which checks
for operating system support. It can be enabled and disabled on-the-fly with

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html)

`enable()`[and via a dynamic condition with](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)

`disable()`[.](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html)

`whenever()`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Styling is enabled by default.
assert!(yansi::is_enabled());
// Disable it with `Painted::disable()`.
yansi::disable();
assert!(!yansi::is_enabled());
// Reenable with `Painted::enable()`.
yansi::enable();
assert!(yansi::is_enabled());
```

# pretty_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty_assertions/latest/target-redirect/pretty_assertions/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#pretty-assertions)Pretty Assertions

When writing tests in Rust, you’ll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` *a lot*.

If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`.
But you have to spot the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward,
like here:

Wouldn’t that task be *much* easier with a colorful diff?

Yep — and you only need **one line of code** to make it happen:

`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`## Show the example behind the screenshots above.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// 1. add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
// 2. insert this line at the top of each module, as needed
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Foo {
    lorem: &'static str,
    ipsum: u32,
    dolor: Result<String, String>,
}
let x = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello World!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey".to_string())});
let y = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello Wrold!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey ho!".to_string())});
assert_eq!(x, y);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#tip)Tip

Specify it as [ [dev-dependencies]](http://doc.crates.io/specifying-dependencies.html#development-dependencies)
and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
This way the compile time of

`cargo build` won’t be affected!Also add `#[cfg(test)]` to your `use` statements, like this:

```
#[cfg(test)]
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

- Since `Rust 2018`edition, you need to declare`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`per module. Before you would write`#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions;`.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.
- `assert_ne`is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does- *not*show a diff.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Features provided by the crate are:

- `std`: Use the Rust standard library. Enabled by default. Exactly one of- `std`and- `alloc`is required.
- `alloc`: Use the- `alloc`crate. Exactly one of- `std`and- `alloc`is required.
- `unstable`: opt-in to unstable features that may not follow Semantic Versioning. The implementation behind this feature is subject to change without warning between patch versions.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq.html)- eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_matches.html)- matches
- Asserts that a value matches a pattern.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_ne.html)- ne
- Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_str_eq.html)- str_ - eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using `PartialEq`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Comparison](https://docs.rs/struct.Comparison.html)
- A comparison of two values.
- [StrComparison](https://docs.rs/struct.StrComparison.html)
- A comparison of two strings.

# pretty_assertions/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # Pretty Assertions
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! When writing tests in Rust, you'll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` _a lot_.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! But you have to spot the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward,
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! like here:
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ![standard assertion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rust-pretty-assertions/rust-pretty-assertions/2d2357ff56d22c51a86b2f1cfe6efcee9f5a8081/examples/standard_assertion.png)
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! Wouldn't that task be _much_ easier with a colorful diff?
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! ![pretty assertion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rust-pretty-assertions/rust-pretty-assertions/2d2357ff56d22c51a86b2f1cfe6efcee9f5a8081/examples/pretty_assertion.png)
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! Yep — and you only need **one line of code** to make it happen:
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! ```rust
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! ```
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! <details>
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! <summary>Show the example behind the screenshots above.</summary>
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! ```rust,should_panic
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! // 1. add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! // 2. insert this line at the top of each module, as needed
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! struct Foo {
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!     lorem: &'static str,
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!     ipsum: u32,
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!     dolor: Result<String, String>,
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! }
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! let x = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello World!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey".to_string())});
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! let y = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello Wrold!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey ho!".to_string())});
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! assert_eq!(x, y);
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! ```
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! </details>
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! ## Tip
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! Specify it as [`[dev-dependencies]`](http://doc.crates.io/specifying-dependencies.html#development-dependencies)
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! This way the compile time of `cargo build` won't be affected!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! Also add `#[cfg(test)]` to your `use` statements, like this:
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ```rust
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! #[cfg(test)]
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! ```
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! ## Note
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! * Since `Rust 2018` edition, you need to declare
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!   `use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};` per module.
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!   Before you would write `#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions;`.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! * The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!   you include.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! * `assert_ne` is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does _not_ show
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!   a diff.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! ## Features
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! Features provided by the crate are:
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! - `std`: Use the Rust standard library. Enabled by default.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!   Exactly one of `std` and `alloc` is required.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! - `alloc`: Use the `alloc` crate.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!   Exactly one of `std` and `alloc` is required.
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! - `unstable`: opt-in to unstable features that may not follow Semantic Versioning.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!   The implementation behind this feature is subject to change without warning between patch versions.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)
[77](https://docs.rs#77)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]
[78](https://docs.rs#78)#![deny(clippy::all, missing_docs, unsafe_code)]
[79](https://docs.rs#79)
[80](https://docs.rs#80)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[81](https://docs.rs#81)#[macro_use]
[82](https://docs.rs#82)extern crate alloc;
[83](https://docs.rs#83)use core::fmt::{self, Debug, Display};

[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// A comparison of two values.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///
[89](https://docs.rs#89)/// Where both values implement `Debug`, the comparison can be displayed as a pretty diff.
[90](https://docs.rs#90)///
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// ```
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// use pretty_assertions::Comparison;
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// print!("{}", Comparison::new(&123, &134));
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// ```
[96](https://docs.rs#96)///
[97](https://docs.rs#97)/// The values may have different types, although in practice they are usually the same.
[98](https://docs.rs#98)pub struct Comparison<'a, TLeft, TRight>
[99](https://docs.rs#99)where
[100](https://docs.rs#100)    TLeft: ?Sized,
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    TRight: ?Sized,
[102](https://docs.rs#102){
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    left: &'a TLeft,
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    right: &'a TRight,
[105](https://docs.rs#105)}
[106](https://docs.rs#106)
[107](https://docs.rs#107)impl<'a, TLeft, TRight> Comparison<'a, TLeft, TRight>
[108](https://docs.rs#108)where
[109](https://docs.rs#109)    TLeft: ?Sized,
[110](https://docs.rs#110)    TRight: ?Sized,
[111](https://docs.rs#111){
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    /// Store two values to be compared in future.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    ///
[114](https://docs.rs#114)    /// Expensive diffing is deferred until calling `Debug::fmt`.
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    pub fn new(left: &'a TLeft, right: &'a TRight) -> Comparison<'a, TLeft, TRight> {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)        Comparison { left, right }
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    }
[118](https://docs.rs#118)}
[119](https://docs.rs#119)
[120](https://docs.rs#120)impl<'a, TLeft, TRight> Display for Comparison<'a, TLeft, TRight>
[121](https://docs.rs#121)where
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    TLeft: Debug + ?Sized,
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    TRight: Debug + ?Sized,
[124](https://docs.rs#124){
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[126](https://docs.rs#126)        // To diff arbitary types, render them as debug strings
[127](https://docs.rs#127)        let left_debug = format!("{:#?}", self.left);
[128](https://docs.rs#128)        let right_debug = format!("{:#?}", self.right);
[129](https://docs.rs#129)        // And then diff the debug output
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        printer::write_header(f)?;
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        printer::write_lines(f, &left_debug, &right_debug)
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    }
[133](https://docs.rs#133)}

[135](https://docs.rs#135)/// A comparison of two strings.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///
[137](https://docs.rs#137)/// In contrast to [`Comparison`], which uses the [`core::fmt::Debug`] representation,
[138](https://docs.rs#138)/// `StrComparison` uses the string values directly, resulting in multi-line output for multiline strings.
[139](https://docs.rs#139)///
[140](https://docs.rs#140)/// ```
[141](https://docs.rs#141)/// use pretty_assertions::StrComparison;
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///
[143](https://docs.rs#143)/// print!("{}", StrComparison::new("foo\nbar", "foo\nbaz"));
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// ```
[145](https://docs.rs#145)///
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// ## Value type bounds
[147](https://docs.rs#147)///
[148](https://docs.rs#148)/// Any value that can be referenced as a [`str`] via [`AsRef`] may be used:
[149](https://docs.rs#149)///
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// ```
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// use pretty_assertions::StrComparison;
[152](https://docs.rs#152)///
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// #[derive(PartialEq)]
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// struct MyString(String);
[155](https://docs.rs#155)///
[156](https://docs.rs#156)/// impl AsRef<str> for MyString {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)///     fn as_ref(&self) -> &str {
[158](https://docs.rs#158)///         &self.0
[159](https://docs.rs#159)///     }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// }
[161](https://docs.rs#161)///
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// print!(
[163](https://docs.rs#163)///     "{}",
[164](https://docs.rs#164)///     StrComparison::new(
[165](https://docs.rs#165)///         &MyString("foo\nbar".to_owned()),
[166](https://docs.rs#166)///         &MyString("foo\nbaz".to_owned()),
[167](https://docs.rs#167)///     ),
[168](https://docs.rs#168)/// );
[169](https://docs.rs#169)/// ```
[170](https://docs.rs#170)///
[171](https://docs.rs#171)/// The values may have different types, although in practice they are usually the same.

[177](https://docs.rs#177)    left: &'a TLeft,
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    right: &'a TRight,
[179](https://docs.rs#179)}

[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using [`PartialEq`]).
[206](https://docs.rs#206)///
[207](https://docs.rs#207)/// On panic, this macro will print a diff derived from [`Debug`] representation of
[208](https://docs.rs#208)/// each value.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)///
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// This is a drop in replacement for [`core::assert_eq!`].
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// You can provide a custom panic message if desired.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)///
[213](https://docs.rs#213)/// # Examples
[214](https://docs.rs#214)///
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// ```
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// use pretty_assertions::assert_eq;
[217](https://docs.rs#217)///
[218](https://docs.rs#218)/// let a = 3;
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// let b = 1 + 2;
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// assert_eq!(a, b);
[221](https://docs.rs#221)///
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// assert_eq!(a, b, "we are testing addition with {} and {}", a, b);
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// ```
[224](https://docs.rs#224)#[macro_export]
[225](https://docs.rs#225)macro_rules! assert_eq {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    ($left:expr, $right:expr$(,)?) => ({
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        $crate::assert_eq!(@ $left, $right, "", "");
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    });
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ($left:expr, $right:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => ({
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        $crate::assert_eq!(@ $left, $right, ": ", $($arg)+);
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    });
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    (@ $left:expr, $right:expr, $maybe_colon:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => ({
[233](https://docs.rs#233)        match (&($left), &($right)) {
[234](https://docs.rs#234)            (left_val, right_val) => {
[235](https://docs.rs#235)                if !(*left_val == *right_val) {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)                    use $crate::private::CreateComparison;
[237](https://docs.rs#237)                    ::core::panic!("assertion failed: `(left == right)`{}{}\
[238](https://docs.rs#238)                       \n\
[239](https://docs.rs#239)                       \n{}\
[240](https://docs.rs#240)                       \n",
[241](https://docs.rs#241)                       $maybe_colon,
[242](https://docs.rs#242)                       format_args!($($arg)*),
[243](https://docs.rs#243)                       (left_val, right_val).create_comparison()
[244](https://docs.rs#244)                    )
[245](https://docs.rs#245)                }
[246](https://docs.rs#246)            }
[247](https://docs.rs#247)        }
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    });
[249](https://docs.rs#249)}
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)/// Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using [`PartialEq`]).
[252](https://docs.rs#252)///
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// On panic, this macro will print a diff derived from each value's [`str`] representation.
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// See [`StrComparison`] for further details.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// This is a drop in replacement for [`core::assert_eq!`].
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// You can provide a custom panic message if desired.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)/// # Examples
[260](https://docs.rs#260)///
[261](https://docs.rs#261)/// ```
[262](https://docs.rs#262)/// use pretty_assertions::assert_str_eq;
[263](https://docs.rs#263)///
[264](https://docs.rs#264)/// let a = "foo\nbar";
[265](https://docs.rs#265)/// let b = ["foo", "bar"].join("\n");
[266](https://docs.rs#266)/// assert_str_eq!(a, b);
[267](https://docs.rs#267)///
[268](https://docs.rs#268)/// assert_str_eq!(a, b, "we are testing concatenation with {} and {}", a, b);
[269](https://docs.rs#269)/// ```
[270](https://docs.rs#270)#[macro_export]
[271](https://docs.rs#271)macro_rules! assert_str_eq {
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    ($left:expr, $right:expr$(,)?) => ({
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        $crate::assert_str_eq!(@ $left, $right, "", "");
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    });
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ($left:expr, $right:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => ({
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        $crate::assert_str_eq!(@ $left, $right, ": ", $($arg)+);
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    });
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    (@ $left:expr, $right:expr, $maybe_colon:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => ({
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        match (&($left), &($right)) {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)            (left_val, right_val) => {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)                if !(*left_val == *right_val) {
[282](https://docs.rs#282)                    ::core::panic!("assertion failed: `(left == right)`{}{}\
[283](https://docs.rs#283)                       \n\
[284](https://docs.rs#284)                       \n{}\
[285](https://docs.rs#285)                       \n",
[286](https://docs.rs#286)                       $maybe_colon,
[287](https://docs.rs#287)                       format_args!($($arg)*),
[288](https://docs.rs#288)                       $crate::StrComparison::new(left_val, right_val)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)                    )
[290](https://docs.rs#290)                }
[291](https://docs.rs#291)            }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        }
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    });
[294](https://docs.rs#294)}
[295](https://docs.rs#295)
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other (using [`PartialEq`]).
[297](https://docs.rs#297)///
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// On panic, this macro will print the values of the expressions with their
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// [`Debug`] representations.
[300](https://docs.rs#300)///
[301](https://docs.rs#301)/// This is a drop in replacement for [`core::assert_ne!`].
[302](https://docs.rs#302)/// You can provide a custom panic message if desired.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)///
[304](https://docs.rs#304)/// # Examples
[305](https://docs.rs#305)///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)/// ```
[307](https://docs.rs#307)/// use pretty_assertions::assert_ne;
[308](https://docs.rs#308)///
[309](https://docs.rs#309)/// let a = 3;
[310](https://docs.rs#310)/// let b = 2;
[311](https://docs.rs#311)/// assert_ne!(a, b);
[312](https://docs.rs#312)///
[313](https://docs.rs#313)/// assert_ne!(a, b, "we are testing that the values are not equal");
[314](https://docs.rs#314)/// ```
[315](https://docs.rs#315)#[macro_export]
[316](https://docs.rs#316)macro_rules! assert_ne {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    ($left:expr, $right:expr$(,)?) => ({
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        $crate::assert_ne!(@ $left, $right, "", "");
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    });
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    ($left:expr, $right:expr, $($arg:tt)+) => ({
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        $crate::assert_ne!(@ $left, $right, ": ", $($arg)+);
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    });
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    (@ $left:expr, $right:expr, $maybe_colon:expr, $($arg:tt)+) => ({
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        match (&($left), &($right)) {
[325](https://docs.rs#325)            (left_val, right_val) => {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)                if *left_val == *right_val {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)                    ::core::panic!("assertion failed: `(left != right)`{}{}\
[328](https://docs.rs#328)                        \n\
[329](https://docs.rs#329)                        \nBoth sides:\
[330](https://docs.rs#330)                        \n{:#?}\
[331](https://docs.rs#331)                        \n\
[332](https://docs.rs#332)                        \n",
[333](https://docs.rs#333)                        $maybe_colon,
[334](https://docs.rs#334)                        format_args!($($arg)+),
[335](https://docs.rs#335)                        left_val
[336](https://docs.rs#336)                    )
[337](https://docs.rs#337)                }
[338](https://docs.rs#338)            }
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        }
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    });

[342](https://docs.rs#342)
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// Asserts that a value matches a pattern.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// On panic, this macro will print a diff derived from [`Debug`] representation of
[346](https://docs.rs#346)/// the value, and a string representation of the pattern.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)///
[348](https://docs.rs#348)/// This is a drop in replacement for [`core::assert_matches::assert_matches!`].
[349](https://docs.rs#349)/// You can provide a custom panic message if desired.
[350](https://docs.rs#350)///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)/// # Examples
[352](https://docs.rs#352)///
[353](https://docs.rs#353)/// ```
[354](https://docs.rs#354)/// use pretty_assertions::assert_matches;
[355](https://docs.rs#355)///
[356](https://docs.rs#356)/// let a = Some(3);
[357](https://docs.rs#357)/// assert_matches!(a, Some(_));
[358](https://docs.rs#358)///
[359](https://docs.rs#359)/// assert_matches!(a, Some(value) if value > 2, "we are testing {:?} with a pattern", a);
[360](https://docs.rs#360)/// ```
[361](https://docs.rs#361)///
[362](https://docs.rs#362)/// # Features
[363](https://docs.rs#363)///
[364](https://docs.rs#364)/// Requires the `unstable` feature to be enabled.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)/// **Please note:** implementation under the `unstable` feature may be changed between
[367](https://docs.rs#367)/// patch versions without warning.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)#[cfg(feature = "unstable")]
[369](https://docs.rs#369)#[macro_export]
[370](https://docs.rs#370)macro_rules! assert_matches {
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    ($left:expr, $( $pattern:pat )|+ $( if $guard: expr )? $(,)?) => ({
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        match $left {
[373](https://docs.rs#373)            $( $pattern )|+ $( if $guard )? => {}
[374](https://docs.rs#374)            ref left_val => {

# assert_eq in pretty_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty_assertions/latest/target-redirect/pretty_assertions/macro.assert_eq.html

```
macro_rules! assert_eq {
    ($left:expr, $right:expr$(,)?) => { ... };
    ($left:expr, $right:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
    (@ $left:expr, $right:expr, $maybe_colon:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using [ PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialEq.html)).

On panic, this macro will print a diff derived from [ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) representation of
each value.

This is a drop in replacement for [ core::assert_eq!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.assert_eq.html).
You can provide a custom panic message if desired.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use pretty_assertions::assert_eq;
let a = 3;
let b = 1 + 2;
assert_eq!(a, b);
assert_eq!(a, b, "we are testing addition with {} and {}", a, b);
```

---

# assert_matches in pretty_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty_assertions/latest/target-redirect/pretty_assertions/macro.assert_matches.html

```
macro_rules! assert_matches {
    ($left:expr, $( $pattern:pat )|+ $( if $guard: expr )? $(,)?) => { ... };
    ($left:expr, $( $pattern:pat )|+ $( if $guard: expr )?, $($arg:tt)+) => { ... };
    (@ $left:expr, $right:expr, $maybe_colon:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Asserts that a value matches a pattern.

On panic, this macro will print a diff derived from [ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) representation of
the value, and a string representation of the pattern.

This is a drop in replacement for [`core::assert_matches::assert_matches!`].
You can provide a custom panic message if desired.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use pretty_assertions::assert_matches;
let a = Some(3);
assert_matches!(a, Some(_));
assert_matches!(a, Some(value) if value > 2, "we are testing {:?} with a pattern", a);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Requires the `unstable` feature to be enabled.

**Please note:** implementation under the `unstable` feature may be changed between
patch versions without warning.

---

# assert_ne in pretty_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty_assertions/latest/target-redirect/pretty_assertions/macro.assert_ne.html

```
macro_rules! assert_ne {
    ($left:expr, $right:expr$(,)?) => { ... };
    ($left:expr, $right:expr, $($arg:tt)+) => { ... };
    (@ $left:expr, $right:expr, $maybe_colon:expr, $($arg:tt)+) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other (using [ PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialEq.html)).

On panic, this macro will print the values of the expressions with their
[ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) representations.

This is a drop in replacement for [ core::assert_ne!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.assert_ne.html).
You can provide a custom panic message if desired.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use pretty_assertions::assert_ne;
let a = 3;
let b = 2;
assert_ne!(a, b);
assert_ne!(a, b, "we are testing that the values are not equal");
```

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
