# crabgrind - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/0.2.7/crabgrind/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#summary)Summary

`crabgrind` is a small library that enables Rust programs to tap into
Valgrind’s tools and environment.

It exposes full set of [Valgrind’s client requests](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/manual-core-adv.html#manual-core-adv.clientreq) in Rust,
manages the structure, type conversions and enforces static typing where
possible.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

**Minimum Supported Rust Version:** 1.71

First, add `crabgrind` as a dependency in `Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
crabgrind = "0.3"
```
or

`cargo add crabgrind`Note: This crate is

`no_std`and dependency-free

[§](https://docs.rs#build-configuration)Build Configuration

The crate needs access to a local Valgrind installation(or at least its headers) in order to read C macro definitions, constants, and supported requests.

The build script (`build.rs`) attempts to locate headers in this order:

- **Environment Variable:**If- `VALGRIND_INCLUDE`is set, it’s value is added to the search paths.
- **pkg-config:**The system is queried via- `pkg-config`.
- **Compiler defaults:**No additional include paths are provided, and the compiler’s default include paths are used.

If headers cannot be located, the crate will still compile without errors, however any request will panic at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Use some of the [Client Requests](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/#modules):

```
use crabgrind::valgrind::{running_mode, RunningMode};
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(
        running_mode(), RunningMode::Valgrind,
        ":~$ valgrind {}", std::env::current_exe().unwrap().display()
    );
    crabgrind::println!("Hey, Valgrind!");
}
```
And run under Valgrind

`:~$ cargo build :~$ valgrind ./target/debug/app`

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- **valgrind**- *(default)*Enables execution of requests, C-shim compilation and bindings generation.

With `default-features = false`, all requests turn into no-op stubs and are
optimized out by the compiler. No build dependencies are pulled in.

```
[dependencies]
crabgrind = { version = "0.3", default-features = false }
[build-dependencies]
crabgrind = "0.3"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more-examples)More Examples

- [Valgrind: Deterministic regression testing(e.g. CI or unit tests)](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/valgrind/fn.count_errors.html#example)
- [Callgrind: Profiling specific code blocks in isolation](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/callgrind/fn.toggle_collect.html#example)
- [Callgrind: Clearing setup costs to isolate some operation](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/callgrind/fn.zero_stats.html#example)
- [Memcheck: Checking for memory leaks at runtime(e.g. CI or unit tests)](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/memcheck/fn.leak_check.html#example)
- [Memcheck: Enforcing bounds in a custom allocator](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/memcheck/fn.mark_memory.html#example)
- [Memcheck: Checking for memory ‘definedness’ feat. MaybeUninit](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/memcheck/fn.check_mem_defined.html#example)
- [DHAT: Tracking data volumes](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/dhat/fn.ad_hoc_event.html#example)
- [DRD: Tracking races in a custom shared memory](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/drd/fn.annotate_new_memory.html#example)
- [DRD: Tracing memory accesses over some memory](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/drd/fn.trace_var.html#example)

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

[Valgrind’s client request](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/manual-core-adv.html#manual-core-adv.clientreq) mechanism is a C implementation
detail, exposed strictly via C macros. Since Rust does not support C
preprocessor, these macros cannot be used directly.

`crabgrind` wraps the foundational `VALGRIND_DO_CLIENT_REQUEST_EXPR` macro via
FFI binding. All higher-level client requests are implemented in Rust on top of
this binding.

The overhead per request, compared to using C macros directly is strictly the cost of a single function call.

The implementation is independent of any specific Valgrind version. Instead, mismatches between requests and local Valgrind instance are handled at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-behavior)Runtime Behavior

We are coupled to the Valgrind version present during compilation.

If a request is invoked at runtime that is unsupported by the active Valgrind instance (e.g. running under an older Valgrind), the call panics immediately, showing the version mismatch message and request requirements.

If your application is running **without** Valgrind, these
requests execute as harmless machine code. They will not panic or segfault, and
overhead is probably undetectable except in a tight loops.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

`crabgrind` is distributed under `MIT` license.

`Valgrind` itself is a GPL3, however `valgrind/*.h` headers are distributed
under a BSD-style license, so we can use them without worrying about license
conflicts.

Valgrind’s tools and environment.

It exposes full set of [Valgrind’s client requests](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/manual-core-adv.html#manual-core-adv.clientreq) in Rust,
manages the structure, type conversions and enforces static typing where
possible.

[§](https://docs.rs#build-configuration)Build Configuration

The crate needs access to a local Valgrind installation(or at least its headers) in order to read C macro definitions, constants, and supported requests.

The build script (`build.rs`) attempts to locate headers in this order:

- **Environment Variable:**If- `VALGRIND_INCLUDE`is set, it’s value is added to the search paths.
- **pkg-config:**The system is queried via- `pkg-config`.
- **Compiler defaults:**No additional include paths are provided, and the compiler’s default include paths are used.

If headers cannot be located, the crate will still compile without errors, however any request will panic at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Use some of the [Client Requests](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/#modules):

```
use crabgrind::valgrind::{running_mode, RunningMode};
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(
        running_mode(), RunningMode::Valgrind,
        ":~$ valgrind {}", std::env::current_exe().unwrap().display()
    );
    crabgrind::println!("Hey, Valgrind!");
}
```
And run under Valgrind

`:~$ cargo build :~$ valgrind ./target/debug/app`

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- **valgrind**- *(default)*Enables execution of requests, C-shim compilation and bindings generation.

With `default-features = false`, all requests turn into no-op stubs and are
optimized out by the compiler. No build dependencies are pulled in.

```
[dependencies]
crabgrind = { version = "0.3", default-features = false }
[build-dependencies]
crabgrind = "0.3"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more-examples)More Examples

- [Valgrind: Deterministic regression testing(e.g. CI or unit tests)](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/valgrind/fn.count_errors.html#example)
- [Callgrind: Profiling specific code blocks in isolation](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/callgrind/fn.toggle_collect.html#example)
- [Callgrind: Clearing setup costs to isolate some operation](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/callgrind/fn.zero_stats.html#example)
- [Memcheck: Checking for memory leaks at runtime(e.g. CI or unit tests)](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/memcheck/fn.leak_check.html#example)
- [Memcheck: Enforcing bounds in a custom allocator](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/memcheck/fn.mark_memory.html#example)
- [Memcheck: Checking for memory ‘definedness’ feat. MaybeUninit](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/memcheck/fn.check_mem_defined.html#example)
- [DHAT: Tracking data volumes](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/dhat/fn.ad_hoc_event.html#example)
- [DRD: Tracking races in a custom shared memory](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/drd/fn.annotate_new_memory.html#example)
- [DRD: Tracing memory accesses over some memory](https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/drd/fn.trace_var.html#example)

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

[Valgrind’s client request](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/manual-core-adv.html#manual-core-adv.clientreq) mechanism is a C implementation
detail, exposed strictly via C macros. Since Rust does not support C
preprocessor, these macros cannot be used directly.

`crabgrind` wraps the foundational `VALGRIND_DO_CLIENT_REQUEST_EXPR` macro via
FFI binding. All higher-level client requests are implemented in Rust on top of
this binding.

The overhead per request, compared to using C macros directly is strictly the cost of a single function call.

The implementation is independent of any specific Valgrind version. Instead, mismatches between requests and local Valgrind instance are handled at compile-time.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-behavior)Runtime Behavior

We are coupled to the Valgrind version present during compilation.

If a request is invoked at runtime that is unsupported by the active Valgrind instance (e.g. running under an older Valgrind), the call panics immediately, showing the version mismatch message and request requirements.

If your application is running **without** Valgrind, these
requests execute as harmless machine code. They will not panic or segfault, and
overhead is probably undetectable except in a tight loops.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

`crabgrind` is distributed under `MIT` license.

`Valgrind` itself is a GPL3, however `valgrind/*.h` headers are distributed
under a BSD-style license, so we can use them without worrying about license
conflicts.

# count_errors in crabgrind::valgrind - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/valgrind/fn.count_errors.html

`pub fn count_errors() -> `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html)## Expand description

Retrieval of the error count recorded by the Valgrind tool

This function wraps the `VALGRIND_COUNT_ERRORS` macro. It returns the current
count of errors encountered during execution.

[§](https://docs.rs#tool-specifics)Tool Specifics

The return value depends entirely on the active tool. Tools that report errors (e.g., Memcheck) return a non-zero count. Tools that do not report errors in the traditional sense (e.g., Cachegrind) will always return zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This is primarily useful in automated test harnesses. When combined with the
`--log-fd=-1` option, Valgrind runs silently (redirecting log output away from
stderr), allowing the client program to inspect the error count
programmatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Deterministic regression testing:

Running Valgrind is often a manual step: run the binary, scroll through the log,
and hope for “ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors”. The [ count_errors](https://docs.rs/fn.count_errors.html) request allows
automating assertions that fail if Valgrind detects any issues.

```
use crabgrind::valgrind as vg;
#[inline(never)]
unsafe fn buggy_ffi(lets_fail: bool) {
    if lets_fail {
        // Simulate a fault Valgrind would catch (e.g. read out of bounds),
        // this triggers an error count increment.
        let v = vec![0u8; 3];
        let p = v.as_ptr().add(v.len());
        std::ptr::read_volatile(p);
    }
}
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    #[test]
    fn test_buggy_ffi() {
        let errors_before = vg::count_errors();
        unsafe { buggy_ffi(false) };
        assert_eq!(errors_before, vg::count_errors());
        unsafe { buggy_ffi(true) };
        assert!(vg::count_errors() > errors_before);
    }
}
```
Run with Memcheck

`:~$ valgrind --tool=memcheck target/debug/count_errors`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Requires Valgrind **3.0** or higher.

# toggle_collect in crabgrind::callgrind - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/callgrind/fn.toggle_collect.html

`pub fn toggle_collect()`## Expand description

Toggling of Profiling Event Recording

Switches the counter collection state on or off. When collection is disabled,
the instrumented code still executes with full overhead, but the counters are
not incremented. This is useful for ignoring specific code sections without the
cost of flushing Valgrind’s translation cache (unlike
[ stop_instrumentation](https://docs.rs/fn.stop_instrumentation.html)).

You can disable collection at startup using the Callgrind option
[–collect-atstart=no](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/cl-manual.html#opt.collect-atstart).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Profiling specific code blocks in isolation:

```
use crabgrind::callgrind;
use std::collections::HashMap;
macro_rules! collect {
    ($expr:expr) => {{
        callgrind::toggle_collect();
        let ret = $expr;
        callgrind::toggle_collect();
        ret
    }}
}
// Profile only the insertion, ignoring setup overhead
let mut map: HashMap<i32, i32> = HashMap::with_capacity(32);
collect!(map.insert(0, 0));
map.shrink_to_fit(); // Ignored by profiler
collect!(map.entry(2).insert_entry(0));
callgrind::dump_stats(None);
```
Run with Callgrind and

[disabled collection](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/cl-manual.html#opt.collect-atstart)`:~$ valgrind --tool=callgrind --collect-atstart=no target/debug/toggle_collect`The resulting dump file can be quickly examined using the

[callgrind_annotate](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/cl-manual.html#cl-manual.callgrind_annotate-options)utility, distributed with Valgrind:`:~$ callgrind_annotate <callgrind_dump_file>`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Requires Valgrind **3.2** or higher.

# zero_stats in crabgrind::callgrind - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/callgrind/fn.zero_stats.html

`pub fn zero_stats()`## Expand description

Reset of Profile Counters

Immediately clears all event counters (instruction fetches, cache misses, etc.) without writing a dump file. It is useful for discarding data from setup phases or previous iterations in a benchmarking loop.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Clearing setup costs to isolate some operation:

```
use crabgrind::callgrind;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::ffi::CStr;
let mut map: HashMap<u8, u8> = HashMap::with_capacity(1024);
let reason = CStr::from_bytes_with_nul(b"HashMap::insert\0").unwrap();
// Reset counters to ignore initialization overhead
callgrind::zero_stats();
// Perform operation we want to measure
map.insert(0, 0);
// Dump isolated data
callgrind::dump_stats(reason);
```
Run with Callgrind

`:~$ valgrind --tool=callgrind target/debug/zero_stats``--666538-- Zeroing costs... --666538-- ...done --666538-- Start dumping at BB 223561 (Client Request: HashMap::insert)... --666538-- Dump to ./callgrind.out.666538.2 --666538-- Dumping done.`

# leak_check in crabgrind::memcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/memcheck/fn.leak_check.html

`pub fn leak_check(check: `[LeakCheck](https://docs.rs/enum.LeakCheck.html))## Expand description

Triggering of a memory leak check at the current execution point

This request bypasses the normal end-of-process leak detection, allowing for granular inspection of memory management in specific subsystems or transient states.

See also [ count_leaks](https://docs.rs/fn.count_leaks.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#behavior)Behavior

The results are emitted directly to the Valgrind output channel (stderr or
XML-file output). Differential modes (`Added`, `Changed`, `New`) rely on state
saved from the immediately preceding leak check.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Checking for memory leaks at runtime:

```
use crabgrind::memcheck as mc;
fn check() -> mc::LeaksCount {
    mc::leak_check(Default::default());
    mc::count_leaks()
    // or equivalently
    // mc::LeakCheck::Full.check()
}
assert_eq!(check().leaked, 0);
// leak 8 bytes
std::mem::forget(vec![0u8; 8]);
assert_eq!(check().leaked, 8);
```
Run with Memcheck

`:~$ valgrind --tool=memcheck target/debug/leak_check`

- `Quick`-- **3.2**

# mark_memory in crabgrind::memcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/memcheck/fn.mark_memory.html

## Expand description

Manipulation of accessibility and validity state for a memory range

This function injects client requests directly into the execution stream to modify Memcheck’s shadow memory. It is useful for custom allocators or optimizing instrumentation of complex memory operations.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Enforcing bounds in a custom allocator:

For custom memory management (e.g. arenas, bump allocators), Memcheck sees only a single large block. Overflows within that block or reading from uninitialized regions only trigger generic ‘uninitialized value’ errors.

By explicitly marking allocated regions as accessible-but-uninitialized
([ MemState::Undefined](https://docs.rs/enum.MemState.html#variant.Undefined)) and restricting access to free space
(

[), we can turn generic errors into precise reports.](https://docs.rs/enum.MemState.html#variant.NoAccess)

`MemState::NoAccess````
use crabgrind::memcheck as mc;
struct BumpAllocator {
    start: *mut u8,
    offset: usize,
    capacity: usize,
}
impl BumpAllocator {
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        let ptr = unsafe {
            libc::mmap(
                std::ptr::null_mut(),
                capacity,
                libc::PROT_READ | libc::PROT_WRITE,
                libc::MAP_ANONYMOUS | libc::MAP_PRIVATE,
                -1,
                0,
            )
        };
        // Mark entire reserved region as inaccessible.
        // This catches stray reads/writes into the "free" part of the arena.
        mc::mark_memory(ptr as _, capacity, mc::MemState::NoAccess);
        // Name the block for better error messages.
        let block_description = std::ffi::CString::new("BumpAllocator").unwrap();
        mc::create_block(ptr as _, capacity, block_description);
        BumpAllocator {
            start: ptr as *mut u8,
            offset: 0,
            capacity,
        }
    }
    fn alloc(&mut self, size: usize) -> *mut u8 {
        let ptr = unsafe { self.start.add(self.offset) };
        // Mark newly allocated slice as "undefined".
        // This allows the program to write to it, but flags uninitialized reads.
        mc::mark_memory(ptr as _, size, mc::MemState::Undefined);
        self.offset += size;
        ptr
    }
}
fn main() {
    let mut bump = BumpAllocator::new(4096);
    let ptr = bump.alloc(100);
    unsafe { ptr.write(42) }; // Valid write.
    // Invalid access:
    // Attempting to write into the gap or the unallocated heap
    // will cause a precise error, rather than a silent corruption.
    unsafe {
        ptr.add(111).write(0);
    }
}
```
Run with Memcheck

`:~$ valgrind --tool=memcheck target/debug/mark_memory`

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

- `NoValgrind`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Requires Valgrind **3.6** for
[ MemState::DefinedIfAddressable](https://docs.rs/enum.MemState.html#variant.DefinedIfAddressable). All other
variants are supported in Valgrind

**3.0**or higher.

# check_mem_defined in crabgrind::memcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/memcheck/fn.check_mem_defined.html

## Expand description

Check of memory range addressability and definedness

This performs an immediate check on both A-bits (addressability) and V-bits (definedness/initialized values) for the specified range. If any byte is not addressable or contains undefined data, Valgrind emits an error report.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::mem::MaybeUninit;
use crabgrind::memcheck;
let mut var = MaybeUninit::<[u8; 2]>::uninit();
let mut vbits = [0u8; 2];
macro_rules! V {
    ($p:expr) => {{
        memcheck::vbits($p as _, vbits.as_mut_slice()).unwrap();
        &vbits[..]
    }};
    () => { V!(var.as_ptr()) };
}
assert_eq!(memcheck::check_mem_defined(var.as_ptr().cast(), 2), Err(0));
assert_eq!(V!(), [0xFF, 0xFF], "all bytes should be 'undefined' at this point");
// Initialize first byte
unsafe { (*var.as_mut_ptr())[0] = 42 };
assert_eq!(memcheck::check_mem_defined(var.as_ptr().cast(), 2), Err(1));
assert_eq!(V!(), [0x0, 0xFF], "only the first byte is 'defined'");
```
Run with Memcheck

`:~$ valgrind --tool=memcheck target/debug/check_mem_defined`

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

- `OffendingOffset`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Requires Valgrind **3.2** or higher.

# ad_hoc_event in crabgrind::dhat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/dhat/fn.ad_hoc_event.html

## Expand description

Recording of a DHAT Ad-Hoc Event

Wraps `DHAT_AD_HOC_EVENT` to record that an event occurred at the current
instruction pointer.

The `weight` argument is an arbitrary unit of measurement that you define:

- `None`- `1`) treats all calls as equally weighted occurrences.
- A `usize`

DHAT aggregates these weights in the profile, showing them as the total “units” attributed to specific call stacks.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Tracking data volumes:

[Ad-hoc mode](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/dh-manual.html#dh-manual.ad-hoc-profiling) generates a flame graph where execution points
are weighted by custom values rather than memory traffic. This can be used for
identifying code paths handling the majority of data volume.

```
use crabgrind::dhat;
// This function logs the length of the input slice. In the DHAT profile,
// this aggregates the total bytes processed per call-site.
fn process_chunk(data: &[u8]) {
    dhat::ad_hoc_event(data.len());
    // simulate processing...
    std::hint::black_box(data);
}
fn main() {
    // A: High frequency, small payloads.
    // 1000 packets of 64 bytes.
    for _ in 0..1_000 {
        process_chunk(&[0u8; 64]);
    }
    // B: Low frequency, massive payloads.
    // 10 packets of ~1 MB.
    for _ in 0..10 {
        process_chunk(&[0u8; 1_000_000]);
    }
}
```
Run with DHAT configured for

[ad-hoc profiling](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/dh-manual.html#dh-manual.ad-hoc-profiling)`:~$ valgrind --tool=dhat --mode=ad-hoc target/debug/ad_hoc_event`The resulting DHAT profile can be quickly examined using the

[dhat-viewer](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/dh-manual.html#dh-manual.viewer)utility, distributed with Valgrind.`... Total: 10,064,000 units (100%, 17,612,264.18/Minstr) in 1,010 events Total: 10,000,000 units (99.4%, 17,500,262.5/Minstr) in 10 events Total: 64,000 units (0.64%, 112,001.68/Minstr) in 1,000 events ...`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Requires Valgrind **3.15** or higher.

This function produces output only when running under Valgrind with DHAT
configured for [ad-hoc profiling](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/dh-manual.html#dh-manual.ad-hoc-profiling):

`:~$ valgrind --tool=dhat --mode=ad-hoc ...`

# annotate_new_memory in crabgrind::drd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/drd/fn.annotate_new_memory.html

## Expand description

Notification of custom memory initialization to DRD

Wraps the `ANNOTATE_NEW_MEMORY` client request.

[§](https://docs.rs#mechanics)Mechanics

DRD automatically tracks memory state by intercepting standard allocation
functions (`malloc`, `free`, `new`, `delete`). If the client program uses a
custom memory allocator (e.g., memory pools, arenas, or direct `mmap`), DRD
treats those memory regions as *unallocated* or *inaccessible*.

This request explicitly informs DRD that the range `[addr, addr+size)` has been
allocated by the application and is now in use. It prevents DRD from reporting
“Invalid read/write” errors on valid custom-allocated memory and ensures race
detection is active for the new block.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Tracking races in custom shared memory:

The following example creates a raw memory mapping (simulating a shared memory segment) and introduces a race condition. DRD will report the race only after the memory is annotated.

```
use libc::{PROT_READ, PROT_WRITE, MAP_ANONYMOUS, MAP_PRIVATE, MAP_FAILED};
use crabgrind::drd;
fn main() {
    const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;
    // Allocate raw memory. DRD does not track this automatically.
    let ptr = unsafe {
        libc::mmap(
            std::ptr::null_mut(),
            PAGE_SIZE,
            PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
            MAP_ANONYMOUS | MAP_PRIVATE,
            -1,
            0
        )
    };
    // Tell DRD to track this memory range.
    drd::annotate_new_memory(ptr as _, PAGE_SIZE);
    // Simulate some race
    let base_addr = ptr as usize;
    let handle1 = std::thread::spawn(move || unsafe {
        *(base_addr as *mut u8) = 1; // Unprotected write
    });
    let handle2 = std::thread::spawn(move || unsafe {
        *(base_addr as *mut u8) = 2; // Unprotected write (Race with Thread 1)
    });
    handle1.join().unwrap();
    handle2.join().unwrap();
    unsafe { libc::munmap(ptr, PAGE_SIZE) };
}
```
Run with DRD

`:~$ valgrind --tool=drd target/debug/annotate_new_memory`Because the range is registered, DRD detects the conflicting access and reports a data race:

`... Conflicting store by thread 3 at 0x04d53ee6 size 1 ...`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Requires Valgrind **3.5** or higher.

# trace_var in crabgrind::drd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/latest/crabgrind/drd/fn.trace_var.html

`pub fn trace_var<T>(var: `[&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html)) -> [ScopeGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeGuard.html)<DRDTracing<'_, T>>## Expand description

Activation of access tracing with a RAII guard

Tracing is immediate. The returned guard manages the duration: tracing stops automatically when the guard is dropped.

This corresponds to the `DRD_TRACE_VAR` and `DRD_STOP_TRACING_VAR` client
requests.

[§](https://docs.rs#mechanics)Mechanics

When active, DRD logs every load and store operation performed on the address
range of `var`. This generates verbose output but provides a granular trace of
access history, which is useful for diagnosing complex race conditions reported
by DRD.

**Warning:** This is an expensive operation in terms of performance and log
volume on the Valgrind side. Use only for targeted debugging.

The lifetime of the guard is tied to `&var`.

Acquiring the guard does **not** hold an active borrow. You may mutate `var`
while the guard is active.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Tracing memory accesses:

```
use crabgrind::drd;
let i: i32 = 0;
// Tell DRD to trace all accesses to the memory behind the reference
let guard = drd::trace_var(&i);
// The following access (read) will be registered by DRD
unsafe { std::ptr::read_volatile(&i as *const _) };
```
Run with DRD

`:~$ valgrind --tool=drd target/debug/trace_var`

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Requires Valgrind **3.3** or higher.

# crabgrind::drd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/0.2.7/crabgrind/drd/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#drd-client-requests)DRD Client Requests

Interface to [DRD Client Requests](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/drd-manual.html#drd-manual.clientreqs) defined in `valgrind/drd.h`.

DRD is a Valgrind tool that detects data races in multithreaded programs by shadowing every memory access. It tracks the synchronization state of threads.

Client requests allow the program to influence DRD’s analysis when static instrumentation is insufficient. They are primarily used to:

- *Suppress false positives:*Identify intentional races or benign unsynchronized accesses (e.g., lock-free counters or statistics).
- *Debug specific regions:*Trace activity on individual variables or memory ranges to pinpoint the origin of complex races.
- *Describe custom logic:*Annotate custom memory allocators or custom synchronization primitives that DRD does not natively recognize.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Nothing happens unless the binary runs under DRD:

`:~$ cargo build :~$ valgrind --tool=drd target/debug/app`

[§](https://docs.rs#version-requirements)Version Requirements

- **Minimum Valgrind:**- `3.3`
- **Recommended Valgrind:**- `3.5`or higher to use any of DRD’s requests

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_benign_race.html)- benign_ - race
- Annotation of a memory address as a “benign race”
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_benign_race_sized.html)- benign_ - race_ - sized
- Annotation of a memory range as a “benign race”
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_ignore_reads.html)- ignore_ - reads
- Suppression of Data Race Reports for memory **reads**
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_ignore_writes.html)- ignore_ - writes
- Suppression of Data Race Reports for memory **writes**
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_new_memory.html)- new_ - memory
- Notification of custom memory initialization to DRD
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_thread_name.html)- thread_ - name
- Assignment of a human-readable name to the current thread
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_trace_memory.html)- trace_ - memory
- Reporting of memory accesses at a specific address
- [drd_](https://docs.rs/fn.drd_threadid.html)- threadid
- Retrieval of the DRD-specific thread ID
- [ignore_](https://docs.rs/fn.ignore_var.html)- var
- Activation of data race suppression
- [trace_](https://docs.rs/fn.trace_var.html)- var

- [valgrind_](https://docs.rs/fn.valgrind_threadid.html)- threadid

# crabgrind::helgrind - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/0.2.7/crabgrind/helgrind/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#helgrind-client-requests)Helgrind Client Requests

Interface to [Helgrind Client Requests](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/hg-manual.html#hg-manual.client-requests) defined in
`valgrind/helgrind.h`.

Helgrind detects data races in multithreaded programs. It natively understands standard POSIX threading primitives, but it relies on these client requests to understand the semantics of user-defined synchronization primitives, memory recycling schemes, or custom atomic operations.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Nothing happens unless the binary runs under Helgrind:

`:~$ cargo build :~$ valgrind --tool=helgrind target/debug/app`

[§](https://docs.rs#version-requirements)Version Requirements

- **Minimum Valgrind:**- `3.2`(required for- `clean_memory`
- **Recommended Valgrind:**- `3.7`or higher to use any of Helgrind’s requests

- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_happens_after.html)- happens_ - after
- Annotation of the “waiter” side of a custom synchronization event
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_happens_before.html)- happens_ - before
- Annotation of the “signaller” side of a custom synchronization event
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_happens_before_forget_all.html)- happens_ - before_ - forget_ - all
- Reset of the synchronization state for a specific object ID
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_rwlock_acquired.html)- rwlock_ - acquired
- Notification of reader-writer lock **acquisition**
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_rwlock_create.html)- rwlock_ - create
- Notification of reader-writer lock **initialization**
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_rwlock_destroy.html)- rwlock_ - destroy
- Notification of reader-writer lock **destruction**
- [annotate_](https://docs.rs/fn.annotate_rwlock_released.html)- rwlock_ - released
- Notification of reader-writer lock **release**
- [clean_](https://docs.rs/fn.clean_memory.html)- memory
- Reset of Helgrind’s tracking state for a specific memory range
- [clean_](https://docs.rs/fn.clean_ref.html)- ref
- Resets Helgrind’s tracking state for a reference.

# crabgrind::memcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crabgrind/0.2.7/crabgrind/memcheck/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#memcheck-client-requests)Memcheck Client Requests

Interface to [Memcheck Client Requests](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/mc-manual.html#mc-manual.clientreqs) defined in
`valgrind/memcheck.h`.

Memcheck detects memory management errors (invalid access, undefined values, leaks). It automatically tracks standard heap allocations, but these client requests are necessary to manually control shadow memory states, perform custom leak detection, or manage non-standard memory allocators.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Nothing happens unless the binary runs under Memcheck:

`:~$ cargo build :~$ valgrind --tool=memcheck target/debug/app`

[§](https://docs.rs#version-requirements)Version Requirements

- **Minimum Valgrind:**- `3.0`
- **Recommended Valgrind:**- `3.6`or higher to use any of Memcheck’s requests

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Leaks](https://docs.rs/struct.LeaksCount.html)- Count
- Aggregated memory leak statistics

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Leak](https://docs.rs/enum.LeakCheck.html)- Check
- Configuration of the scope and output of an immediate leak search
- [MemState](https://docs.rs/enum.MemState.html)
- Representation of the validity state (V-bits) and accessibility (A-bits) for a memory range as tracked by Memcheck’s shadow memory
- [VBits](https://docs.rs/enum.VBitsError.html)- Error
- V-bit (validity bit) manipulation errors.
